verified.reason: Confirmed by source and by an independent runtime probe. withInFlightLimit keys its per-client counter on s.bucketKey(r) = plane + client (middleware.go:459,491-493) while the semaphore is process-wide (middleware.go:434), and perClient = maxInFlight/2 (middleware.go:435). A single client address therefore gets one maxInFlight/2 allowance per plane, and its total across the three planes can equal the whole cap. I wrote a temporary test in package httpapi: Server{maxInFlight:4} (perClient=2), one RemoteAddr issued 2 requests to /oauth/token (planeProtocol) and 2 to /v1/me (planeBusiness); all four slots were held by that one address and a second client address received 503. The rate limiter does not prevent this: it bounds arrivals over time (default 50/s burst 100, config.go:354-355) but not slots held, and per-plane buckets are independent, so ~100 burst + 50/s for ~3s is enough to push in 256 slow requests whose slots are held for the 30s ReadTimeout / 60s WriteTimeout (main.go:117-118). Probes are exempt (middleware.go:455), so /healthz and /readyz stay 200. This defeats the stated guarantee in the comment at middleware.go:423-425 ('at most half of it, and the other half is headroom every other client draws from'). Existing TestInFlightCapIsSharedPerClient only exercises a single plane (/v1/me) and does not cover this. Severity kept at high.

verified.reason: Confirmed by source and by an independent runtime probe. readinessCache.check sets c.running=true and c.settled=make(chan struct{}) before calling probe (health.go:183-186) and clears running / closes settled only on the normal return path after probe returns (health.go:192-194). No defer/recover exists. If probe panics, the panic unwinds out of check with running still true, settled never closed and state still readinessUnknown; every later caller takes the fresh||running branch (health.go:163), sees unknown with a non-nil settled channel, waits readinessColdStartWait and returns unknown (health.go:166-181), so handleReady answers 503 'checking' (health.go:133-138) permanently. I wrote a temporary test in package httpapi: a probe that panics was invoked through handleReady, the panic reached the caller (recoverBrowser at server.go:647 would turn it into a 500), and a subsequent call with a healthy probe still returned 503 body 'checking'. The same wedge occurs for a probe that ignores probeCtx and blocks past readinessTimeout (health.go:188-190 ever returns). Severity medium is appropriate (requires a panicking or non-context-honouring configured probe, but then the instance is permanently drained).

verified.reason: The literal defect is real: Compressor.Handler runs next.ServeHTTP(cw, r) then cw.finish() (compress.go:160-162), and finish() is the only caller of release() (compress.go:292-297,416-423), so a panic that escapes next skips the pooled writer's Close() and Put(). However the finding overstates reachability by citing recoverProtocol/recoverBusiness as evidence that handler panics are a supported path: both of those recoverers sit INSIDE the compression layer. /v1 is mounted as recoverBusiness(s, withNoStore(mux)) (server.go:532,708) and the protocol plane is wrapped once as recoverProtocol(cfg.OIDC) (server.go:331) inside the root mux; the compressor is applied outside the whole tree (server.go:643-644). Therefore protocol- and business-plane panics are recovered before unwinding into compress.Handler and DO reach cw.finish(); only a panic on the browser plane (webui, authMux, /bind, root redirect, 404 handler) escapes to the outermost recoverBrowser (server.go:647), which is outside the compressor, and leaks the writer. Impact is also bounded: the abandoned writer is garbage-collected, so this is pool-refill/allocation churn on a rare path, not an unbounded leak — matching the finding's own 'not externally triggerable' note. Real bug, but narrower than claimed and low impact; severity kept low.

The static facts are correct: Config.Eligible excludes only planeProtocol (server.go:353-355), so business-plane responses are eligible; writeJSON sets Content-Type: application/json and Cache-Control: no-store but never no-transform (responses.go:122-126); compressibleContentType returns true for application/json and no-transform is the skip signal (compress.go:336-339,476-500); CSRFToken is a stable 64-hex-char per-session value (auth.go:240-247,758-764); and /v1/sessions/current and /v1/device/verification include it (session_routes.go:39-44, device_routes.go:75-82). But the concrete exploit chain is much weaker than the finding implies. (1) Compression only engages once the body reaches DefaultMinSize = 1024 bytes (compress.go:25,365-377); the cited reflection endpoint /v1/device/verification emits a body of roughly the 64-char token plus an 8-char code plus a small client object and scope list, typically well under 1024 bytes, so it is normally sent verbatim and provides no compression oracle at all. (2) The 'attacker-supplied input' is not arbitrary: user_code is passed through NormalizeUserCode (device.go:481-483) and then DescribeDeviceAuthorization must succeed (device_routes.go:61-72) before the normalized value is echoed, so an attacker can only reflect a code that already exists in the store, not chosen guess text. (3) Browsers expose no cross-origin response-size oracle, which the finding itself concedes. What remains is a defence-in-depth hardening note (add no-transform to secret-bearing JSON, or exclude CSRF-bearing endpoints), not a practical vulnerability. Downgraded from low to informational.

verified.reason: The performance claim is empirically false in this build. Limiter.Check (ratelimit.go:274-298) does call b.limiter.ReserveN, but the compiler inlines ReserveN and the *Reservation does not escape, so there is no heap allocation. I added a temporary test using testing.AllocsPerRun(2000): Limiter.Check on an existing key = 0 allocs/op, and a raw rate.Limiter.ReserveN+OK+DelayFrom+CancelAt sequence = 0 allocs/op. This is consistent with the x/time comment at rate@v0.16.0/rate.go:336 ('reserveN returns Reservation, not *Reservation, to avoid allocation') combined with inlining of the wrapper (rate.go:227-230); the pointer is stack-allocated, not heap-allocated as the finding asserts from reading the source alone. Existing benchmarks confirm the common path: BenchmarkCheckExistingKey reports 0 allocs/op. The only allocation Check can incur is the creation of a new bucket for a previously unseen key (1-2 allocs in BenchmarkCheckAtCapacity / BenchmarkCheckDistinctKeysParallel), which is unrelated to the reservation. The secondary observation that Check takes the limiter's internal mutex four times (AllowN, TokensAt, ReserveN, CancelAt) is factually right, but the finding's stated impact ('one allocation plus GC pressure per request') and its central recommendation rationale are wrong, so the finding is rejected.

summary: 5 findings independently re-verified against the cited code, callers and an independent runtime probe. Confirmed 2: S10-1 (high) one client address can fill the entire process-wide in-flight semaphore by using two planes because the per-client counter is keyed on (plane, client) while the semaphore is global; reproduced with 2 /oauth/token + 2 /v1/me from one RemoteAddr causing a second address to get 503 at maxInFlight=4. S10-2 (medium) a panicking (or context-ignoring) readiness probe leaves running=true and settled unclosed, wedging /readyz at 503 'checking' forever; reproduced. Downgraded 2: S10-3 real finish()-skipped-on-panic defect but only browser-plane panics escape to recoverBrowser; /v1 and /oauth panics are recovered inside the compression layer, so impact is bounded pool churn (low). S10-4 static compression facts correct but the cited reflection endpoint normally falls under the 1024-byte compression threshold and does not reflect arbitrary attacker text, so no practical oracle (informational). Rejected 1: S10-5's claim that Limiter.Check heap-allocates a *rate.Reservation per request is refuted by AllocsPerRun (0 allocs/op for both Check and raw ReserveN); ReserveN is inlined and the Reservation does not escape. No new severe findings were identified.
